newsitem.title: INDIA: Separatists call for strike over deaths in Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Separatists call for strike over deaths in Kashmir.

text.p: Shops and businesses were closed on Sunday in Srinagar, troubled Kashmir's main city, as a leading separatist group called for a two-day strike to protest the deaths of four militant leaders.
Three leaders of the Hizb-ul-Mujahideen group were killed in a shootout with paramilitary soldiers on Saturday in Jammu and Kashmir state, police said.

Another leader belonging to Hizb-ul-Mujahideen was killed in a gunbattle near Anantnag town, 60 km (35 miles) south of Srinagar, on Thursday evening. Separatist leaders have accused Indian security forces of killing the guerrilla leaders in custody. Police have denied the charge.

"We appeal to the people of Jammu and Kashmir to observe a complete strike on March 9 and March 10 in protest against the custodial killings of four leaders," Hizb-ul-Mujahideen said in a statement distributed to newspaper offices in Srinagar.
Most of the streets in Srinagar were deserted except for security patrols. Sunday is a normal business day in Moslem dominated Kashmir.
Hizb-ul-Mujahideen is fighting for merger of the Himalayan state with neighbouring Pakistan.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have been killed in a seven-year-old separatist rebellion in mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state.

Two of the three wars fought between India and Pakistan since they gained independence in 1947 have been triggered by disputes over the Kashmir region. The surge in Kashmir violence has occurred as India and Pakistan prepare to resume stalled peace talks later this month.

Pakistan announced on Thursday that foreign ministry secretaries of the two governments would meet in New Delhi on March 28-31, and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he hoped to see a positive outcome from the exercise.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Saturday that talks with Pakistan would address all issues of mutual concern.

The last round of talks between the South Asian neighbours was in January 1994. They bogged down because of differences over Kashmir, two-thirds of which is controlled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
New Delhi regards all of the region as an integral part of the Indian union.

But Islamabad, which denies New Delhi's charges of training and arming the rebels, wants the Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite on whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
No agenda has been announced for the March 28-31 meeting. Pakistan has insisted in the past that Kashmir was the "core issue" and must be on the agenda of any India-Pakistan dialogue.
